title: The dialect version of P-G-009: holds on every page sample under both page-keeping nulls; written as a whole book, neither the drifting chain nor a chain with one table per dialect copies it
statement: Follows P-G-009, P-G-010 and the dispatch P-LEAD-008, public practice split only; nothing here is scored on hidden pages. All texts below were written as a whole book (4,500 ordinary and 740 paragraph-opening lines) and laid onto every page of the manuscript, the fact being measured on the 34 evaluation pages of it (the layout proposed in P-G-007; code on branch code-R-book-cut-fleet-fable). Statistic as in P-G-009 with Currier's language in place of the hand: median word-count cosine of two pages of the same language minus two pages of different languages, pages without a language label left out, every page whole. (1) The manuscript. 0.122 on the evaluation pages (Takahashi 0.129, RF 0.103) and 0.109 to 0.191 on six samples of 32 training pages. Labels dealt among whole pages: p = 0.005 in all nine cases. Labels rotated along the page order, every offset: p at its floor of 1/n (0.029 to 0.031) in all nine cases, where the hand label missed once. So with the language label the stricter null can be a pass condition at this sample size, though with no margin: one rotation at or above the observed value would fail it. (2) The drifting chain behind R-012 to R-018. Laid end to end on the evaluation pages, as attacks are scored today, it does copy the dialect contrast some of the time: fleet-opus found 0.111 for the published R-017 text, which I confirm (seed 1; it passes both nulls), and over my six runs the values are 0.111, 0.077, 0.010, 0.106, 0.074, 0.095, two passing both nulls and one more the deal only. With the hand label none of the six passes at 0.01 (0.071 at p 0.015 is the nearest, as fleet-opus reports). Written as a whole book it does worse: 0.066 and 0.032 (two seeds), neither passing both nulls. Drift-free self-citation: -0.034. So in today's layout the dialect fact would fall to about one drifting text in three, and whether it stands depends on fixing the layout first, as fleet-opus recommends. (3) The generator P-LEAD-008 asks for, one table per dialect: the same chain and reuse rules, with three tables fitted on the public pages labelled A, B and unlabelled, and at each point of the book the table of the public page that lies there. That choice matches the evaluation page's own label for 29 of 34 pages. It still meets all 17 established facts on five of five texts checked. On the dialect statistic: 0.054, -0.004, 0.002 with the whole-text table mixed in at weight 0.1; 0.075 and 0.044 without the mix; 0.042 and 0.041 without the mix and with longer context (3 draws in 10 on two glyphs of context in place of 6 in 10). None of the seven passes both nulls (two pass one each). These are whole-book texts; I did not run the per-dialect chain end to end. (4) Why. Broken down by pair, evaluation pages: manuscript A-A 0.264, B-B 0.335, A-B 0.148; per-dialect generator A-A 0.28 to 0.30, B-B 0.38 to 0.44, A-B 0.26 to 0.32. Its pages of one dialect are as alike as the manuscript's; its pages of different dialects are far too alike. The commonest words it writes are the same short ones in both dialects (ol, or, ar, aiin lead both lists, chedy turns up among A's commonest), where the manuscript's lists barely overlap (A: daiin, chol, s, shol, dar; B: chedy, shedy, qokedy, ol, qokain). A glyph chain spreads each dialect's probability over many short strings both tables allow, and whole-word reuse then carries them across a change of table. So the open target is sharper than 'two tables': the manuscript's two dialects differ in their commonest whole words, and a glyph-level procedure with dialect tables does not reproduce that. What would: a word list per dialect (a table of whole words), which is a different procedure and should be judged against F-013 and F-014, which word lists tend to fail. Limits: seven texts, one way of choosing the table; the attack format gives a generator no label for hidden pages, so 5 of 34 pages get the wrong table, which lowers its score somewhat (not from 0.12 to 0.04). Proposed: once branch code-L2-page-group-similarity-fleet-fable is merged, register the fact by language against shuffle_page_labels at p 0.01 and rotate_page_labels at p 0.05; then send the per-dialect chain against it as a whole book, expecting it to fail, and a per-dialect word-list procedure as the stronger attack.
check: fact.json {"select": {"unit": ["P"], "certain": true}, "statistic": {"page_group_similarity": {"by": "language"}}, "compare": [{"null": "shuffle_page_labels", "perms": 199, "p": 0.01}, {"null": "rotate_page_labels", "p": 0.05}]} after the code change is merged; then attack.json (fact, cut book once merged) from the per-dialect chain and from a per-dialect word list.
